alt: The M’Naghten Rules in three parts: a defect of reason (not mere absent-mindedness, Clarke); from a disease of the mind, an internal cause such as arteriosclerosis, epilepsy, hyperglycaemia or sleepwalking; so that the defendant did not know the nature and quality of the act or that it was legally wrong (Windle). The verdict is not guilty by reason of insanity, followed by a hospital order, supervision order or absolute discharge.
caption: Defect of reason, disease of the mind, and not knowing what or that it was wrong.

alt: Automatism needs an external cause, such as a blow, a reflex (Hill v Baxter), hypoglycaemia from insulin (Quick) or PTSD after a rape (R v T), and a total loss of voluntary control (A-G’s Reference No 2 of 1992). If self-induced: alcohol or illegal drugs bring in the intoxication rules (Lipman); for specific intent it can be a defence; for basic intent it fails if the defendant knew the risk (Bailey) but may succeed if not (Hardie).
caption: External cause and total loss of control; if self-induced, recklessness defeats it for basic intent.

alt: A decision tree. Voluntary intoxication: a defence to specific intent offences if no intent was formed (Beard); no defence to basic intent offences (Majewski); no defence after Dutch courage (Gallagher). Involuntary intoxication: a defence to any offence if no mens rea formed, but none if it was formed (Kingston); sedatives taken normally count as involuntary unless the risk was known (Hardie). Allen and the rule on intoxicated mistakes are noted below.
caption: Voluntary intoxication helps only with specific intent; involuntary only if no mens rea was formed.

alt: Two panels. Hyperglycaemia from failing to take insulin has an internal cause, so it is insanity (Hennessy). Hypoglycaemia from taking insulin without eating enough has an external cause, so it is automatism and an acquittal (Quick). A note records the criticism that diabetics and epileptics are labelled insane.
caption: High blood sugar is insanity; low blood sugar from insulin is automatism.

alt: Ria’s case in five steps: s20 is a basic intent offence; hypoglycaemia from insulin is an external cause, so automatism not insanity (Quick, contrast Hennessy); it must be a total loss of control; she knew the risk, so self-induced automatism is no defence (Bailey); so she may be guilty of s20.
caption: Identify the cause, check total loss of control, then ask whether it was self-induced.
